rationale.Physical Exam: General Appearance: The general examination is extremely useful to determine how sick the patient looks.
rationale.Physical Exam: Chest / Lungs: It's important to look for lung pathology.
rationale.Physical Exam: Abdomen: It's important to look for abdominal pathology.
rationale.Physical Exam: Neuro / Psych: This is the patient's chief complaint — neurologic exam is essential.
rationale.CBC with differential: CBC is always a good screening tool in nearly every patient.
rationale.TSH, serum: TSH screens for abnormal thyroid levels which could contribute to altered mental status.
rationale.CT of head without contrast: CT without contrast is the order of choice. With possible head trauma, rule out intracranial bleed. CT with contrast makes it difficult to distinguish contrast from hemorrhage. CT preferred for speed; MRI more sensitive but slower.
rationale.Basic metabolic profile / Comprehensive: Chemistries are an important screening tool to reach a diagnosis.
rationale.CT, head, with contrast: CT with contrast makes it difficult to distinguish between contrast enhancement and intracranial hemorrhage. Non-contrast CT is the correct choice for suspected bleed.
rationale.Consult, surgery, neurologic / Craniotom: Neurosurgery should be consulted to evacuate the subdural hematoma. Craniotomy for evacuation.
rationale.CT head with contrast: Contrast makes it difficult to distinguish blood from enhancement. Non-contrast CT is required for suspected intracranial hemorrhage.
rationale.Lumbar puncture: LP is contraindicated with suspected mass effect from intracranial hemorrhage — risk of herniation.
rationale.EEG: While seizure is on the differential, CT head takes priority given history of fall and AMS.

hpi: {{patient_name}} is an elderly patient with a history of chronic alcoholism who presents to the emergency department with altered mental status following a recent fall. The patient has had episodic confusion and fluctuating consciousness since the fall. The subdural hematoma risk is elevated due to advanced age and chronic alcohol use, both of which contribute to brain atrophy and increased tension on bridging veins. Time is critical — expanding hematoma may cause mass effect and progressive neurological deterioration.

physical_exam: Fluctuating level of consciousness. Assess for lateralizing signs, pupil asymmetry, and GCS. Focal deficits may indicate mass effect from expanding hematoma.
Assess for signs of head trauma or skull fracture.
Altered mental status — differentiate from psychiatric etiology.

case_summary: Elderly alcoholic patient with fall → subdural hematoma. Subdurals result from venous bleeding after blunt head trauma — bridging veins rupture. Risks: advanced age, alcoholism, anticoagulation. CT without contrast → neurosurgery for evacuation.
